name: SmartOS
summary: A specialized, stateless, in-memory SVR4 hypervisor and cloud operating system built upon illumos, designed for high-density container hosting via Solaris Zones, hardware virtualization via bhyve and KVM, and local OpenZFS storage pools.

content.introduction: SmartOS is an open-source, specialized operating system and type-1 hypervisor derived from the illumos consolidation. Originally engineered by Joyent to power multi-tenant public and private cloud infrastructure, and maintained since 2022 by MNX Solutions within the Triton DataCenter ecosystem, SmartOS combines in-memory execution with enterprise Unix technologies.
content.what_is_it: SmartOS is a purpose-built cloud hypervisor that boots entirely into RAM from USB, ISO, or network PXE media, without ever installing an operating system to disk. It dedicates local physical storage entirely to an OpenZFS pool (named zones) to host virtualized workloads, including native illumos Zones, Linux LX branded zones, and full hardware virtual machines via bhyve and KVM.
content.origin_and_joyent_heritage: Developed by Sun Microsystems alumni at Joyent (notably Bryan Cantrill and Jerry Jelinek), SmartOS extended OpenSolaris into a specialized virtualization appliance. Joyent ported KVM to illumos, engineered LX brand syscall emulation, and created the Triton cloud orchestration stack. Following Joyent's acquisition by Samsung and the subsequent 2022 transfer to MNX Solutions, SmartOS development continues actively under the TritonDataCenter organization.
content.stateless_in_memory_architecture: SmartOS implements a completely stateless, ephemeral bare-metal operating system architecture. The operating system image boots entirely into RAM from a USB flash drive, an ISO image, or via network PXE boot (such as through iPXE). Upon system initialization, the entire root filesystem (`/`) runs directly in memory from a ramdisk. Node-specific configuration variables (such as network IP configuration, admin passwords, and NTP servers) are persistently loaded from a single configuration file located on the boot media (`/usbkey/config`). Because the operating system root is read-only and ephemeral, host reboot always returns the machine to a pristine, uncorrupted software state, eliminating root filesystem drift and administrative host divergence across cluster nodes.
content.virtualization_and_pkgsrc_management: Virtualization on SmartOS operates through a dual-paradigm engine leveraging illumos primitives. For container-style isolation, SmartOS utilizes illumos Zones (OS-level virtualization), providing hardware-level execution speed with near-zero overhead, granular CPU and memory cap controls, and complete filesystem and network isolation via Crossbow VNICs. Software within zones is provisioned via the multi-platform NetBSD pkgsrc package management collection, offering thousands of pre-compiled binaries optimized for illumos. For workloads requiring non-illumos operating systems (such as Linux, FreeBSD, or Microsoft Windows), SmartOS provides full hardware virtualization via bhyve and a tailored illumos port of KVM (Kernel-based Virtual Machine), with virtual disk images backed directly by OpenZFS zvols.
content.deployment_and_datacenter_orchestration: Guest instances and storage assets on SmartOS are managed through JSON-driven command-line interfaces: `vmadm` for provisioning, querying, updating, and destroying virtual machines and zones, and `imgadm` for discovering and pulling standardized image datasets from image repositories. All persistent data resides exclusively on local OpenZFS storage pools (`zpool`, typically named `zones`), benefiting from end-to-end checksumming, native copy-on-write snapshots, and dataset cloning. In large-scale enterprise environments, SmartOS serves as the foundation compute node operating system for the open-source Triton DataCenter (formerly Joyent SmartDataCenter) orchestration platform, while system introspection is powered by DTrace for non-invasive, live production kernel and application tracing.
content.platform_image_release_model_and_install: SmartOS is not versioned like a general-purpose distribution: the smartos-live repository builds a platform image that bundles the illumos core components, a set of extra third-party software and the SmartOS-specific utilities, and the project asks operators to quote the platform version when reporting a problem. The documented installation paths cover writing a downloaded ISO to a USB key, running SmartOS as a VMware, VirtualBox or UTM guest on Apple Silicon, and a non-interactive installation procedure for automated deployment; the running system is then administered with `vmadm` and `imgadm`, with community images taken from a public image server. The project site records the lineage without ambiguity: SmartOS was built and operated by Joyent, Joyent was acquired by Samsung in 2016, and stewardship became independent in 2022 while the code remained open source.
content.lineage_and_stewardship: The project timeline records two ownership changes after the platform was built: Samsung acquired Joyent in 2016, and stewardship changed again in 2022, the platform remaining open source through both transitions. The project links the acquisition announcement and the 2022 post describing the new chapter, and states that Triton Cloud runs on the same platform today.
content.zones_networking_model: Chaque zone dispose de sa propre pile réseau et de ses propres adresses sur le réseau physique. Le projet indique que ce choix supprime la traduction d'adresses, les réseaux superposés et le mappage de ports entre services, chaque zone étant joignable directement.
content.standalone_and_triton_operation: Two operating modes are documented. SmartOS standalone is a single host installed and operated with the vmadm and imgadm command-line tools, using community images from a public image server; Triton adds identity, tenancy, networking, image management, VPCs and an API on top of the same platform. Images provision as ZFS clones, and the same kernel and tooling are used in both modes.
content.security_model_zone_isolation_and_privil: SmartOS documents zones as its isolation boundary. The documentation states that processes cannot escape from a zone, cannot observe processes in other zones and cannot signal them, and that user identifiers or port bindings do not conflict across zones. A process in the global zone can observe any zone when it holds the relevant privilege, whereas a zone process runs under a privilege limit: root inside a zone remains bounded by that limit. Filesystems are mounted from the global zone, which can mount them read-only for a zone, and a zone cannot remount them unless the administrator allows it. Each zone has its own IP stack by default on SmartOS, with a shared-stack mode still available, and kernel-managed resources are polyinstantiated so that each zone keeps its own instance, for example of `/tmp`. Zones have no access to physical devices; hardware is presented as virtualised. Service isolation is provided by SMF. Access control inside the global zone can rely on RBAC: the documentation shows turning root into a role with `usermod -R root`, after which direct root login is no longer possible outside single user mode and only users holding the role may run `su root`, with the persistent configuration kept in `/etc/security/policy.conf`, `auth_attr`, `exec_attr` and `prof_attr`. These pages describe configurable mechanisms and default behaviours; they do not publish a vulnerability response process.
content.platform_build_cadence_and_change_tracki: SmartOS does not publish numbered platform versions. The download documentation states that a new build appears on average every two weeks and is identified by a UTC timestamp of the form `20120809T221258Z`, given in the page example as 08/09/2012 at 22:12:58 UTC. Each build ships five artefacts: the platform archive `platform-<timestamp>.tgz` holding kernel and boot archive, the live ISO `smartos-<timestamp>.iso`, the USB image `smartos-<timestamp>-usb.img.bz2` presented as the preferred method for production hardware, the VMware image `smartos-<timestamp>.vmwarevm.tar.bz2`, and a `SINGLE_USER_ROOT_PASSWORD` text file used only when booting without mounting the zpool. The documentation points to a change log for the contents of each build. Upgrading a USB-key installation is described as a directory swap: the running `platform` directory is retained as `platform.old` and the new one is copied in, which keeps the previous platform available on the key. The same page lists the supported boot paths, including PXE and virtual machines, and states that the build is delivered as an in-memory image whose platform directory can equally be placed on a local disk or served over the network.
advantages: Stateless in-memory architecture guaranteeing immutable host security and effortless platform upgrades
Near-zero overhead multi-tenant container virtualization via native illumos and Linux LX Zones
Full hardware virtualization with integrated bhyve and KVM hypervisors running inside branded zones
Maximized local disk performance dedicating 100% of storage spindles to OpenZFS VM pools
Comprehensive system introspection and low-overhead production profiling via native DTrace
disadvantages: Stateless design requires external storage or specific configuration techniques for persistent host settings
Steep learning curve requiring familiarity with illumos paradigms, vmadm, and JSON manifest provisioning
Strictly limited to 64-bit x86_64 server hardware with hardware virtualization extensions (VT-x or AMD-V)
who_is_it_for: Cloud service providers and enterprise infrastructure teams building high-density virtualization fabrics
DevOps engineers seeking an immutable, hypervisor-grade operating system with native DTrace observability
System administrators managing scalable container and VM clusters via Triton DataCenter
who_is_it_not_for: General-purpose workstation users requiring desktop environments, office tools, or audio/video peripherals
Workloads requiring traditional persistent root disk installations on standalone consumer hardware
content.verdict: SmartOS is a type-1 hypervisor built on illumos, combining OpenZFS and Zones with a stateless in-memory delivery model. It provides observability through DTrace and multi-tenant isolation through Zones, and is used as an open-source platform for cloud computing.
